Knives and flatware pay 25% Section 232; other tools pay the 2026 Section 301 duty; China adds 25%; diamond sawblades carry AD duties.

overview.intro:
Chapter 82 covers tools and cutlery of base metal: garden and farm hand tools, saws and saw blades, files and pliers, wrenches and sockets, hammers, screwdrivers, vises and other hand tools, tool sets, interchangeable tools such as drill bits, dies and milling cutters, machine knives, carbide inserts, hand-operated kitchen appliances, knives, razors, scissors, clippers, and spoons, forks and other flatware. 50 of the 189 lines are **Free** under the general rate; the rest pay up to 12% (slip-joint pliers) or a few cents each plus a percentage (knives, scissors, flatware). Sets pay **the rate of the highest-rated article in the set**.

Two systems decide the extra duty. **52 lines are Section 232 derivative steel articles at 25% of the full value** (9903.82.09) from every country, on top of any FTA or USMCA rate: all knives (8211) and flatware (8215), vises and clamps, iron or steel hand tools of 8205.59.55, pipe and bolt cutters of 8203.40.60 and diamond sawblade cores. Three die and press-tool lines pay a **15% total** Section 232 rate as industrial equipment. The other **134 lines** (wrenches, pliers, hammers, saw blades, drill bits, carbide inserts, scissors, razors) are outside Section 232 and pay the **2026 Section 301** duty instead: 10% or 12.5% for most of the 60 economies, 10% or 12.5% *in place of* the base rate for EU, Japanese, Korean, Swiss and Taiwanese goods, nothing extra for USMCA goods.

China pays another **25%** (List 3) or **7.5%** (List 4A) under Section 301 on most lines; Canadian wrenches, pliers, saw blades, carbide inserts, tool sets and razors pay **50%** under Section 338 even with a USMCA claim. Chinese **diamond sawblades** and **heavy forged hand tools** carry antidumping duties set company by company; they are not part of this table or the tariff calculator (see Tariff updates).

productGroups.label: Garden, farm and forestry hand tools (spades, shovels, picks, hoes, rakes, axes, machetes, pruners, hedge shears)
productGroups.blurb: Spades, shovels, forks and machetes are Free; axes 6.2%; pruners, secateurs and hedge shears 1¢ each + 2.8%. None is on the Section 232 lists. Chinese mattocks, picks and axes also carry the heavy forged hand tools antidumping orders; Canadian picks, hoes and rakes (8201.30) pay 50% under Section 338.

productGroups.label: Saws and saw blades (handsaws, bandsaw, circular, diamond, chain saw and hacksaw blades)
productGroups.blurb: Almost all Free (chromium-alloy chain saw blades 7.2%). Only diamond sawblade cores (8202.39.00.40) are on the Section 232 list, at 25%. Chinese diamond sawblades, cores and segments are under an antidumping order; Canadian steel circular and chain saw blades pay 50% under Section 338.

productGroups.label: Files, pliers, tweezers, metal-cutting shears, pipe and bolt cutters, punches
productGroups.blurb: Files and metal-cutting shears are Free; tweezers 4%, slip-joint pliers 12%, other pliers 12¢/doz. + 5.5%. Pipe cutters, bolt cutters and punches without alloy cutting parts (8203.40.60) are the one Section 232 line (25%).

productGroups.label: Wrenches and spanners (open-end, box, adjustable, torque and socket wrenches, sockets)
productGroups.blurb: Every line pays 9%. Not on the Section 232 lists, so the 2026 Section 301 duties apply (10% in place of the base rate for EU and Taiwanese goods); China adds 25% + 12.5%; Canadian wrenches pay 50% under Section 338 even with a USMCA claim.

productGroups.label: Other hand tools (taps, hammers, chisels, screwdrivers, household tools, crowbars, caulking guns, torches, vises, clamps, anvils and sets)
productGroups.blurb: Base rates mostly Free to 7.2%. Vises and clamps (8205.70) and other iron or steel hand tools of 8205.59.55 are on the Section 232 list at 25%; the rest are not. Sets of 8205.90.60 pay the rate of the highest-rated tool in the set. Chinese hammers over 1.5 kg, bars and wedges carry antidumping orders.

productGroups.label: Tool sets of two or more of headings 8202–8205, put up for retail sale
productGroups.blurb: No fixed rate: a set pays the rate of the article in it with the highest rate (additional U.S. note 3 converts per-unit rates to ad valorem equivalents). Not on the Section 232 list; Chinese sets pay List 3 and the 2026 Section 301 duty on top, Canadian sets 50% under Section 338.

productGroups.label: Interchangeable tools (rock-drilling bits, drill bits, dies, punches, taps, reamers, milling cutters, router bits, turning tools)
productGroups.blurb: Base rates 1.6% to 8.4%. Three lines (parts of drawing dies, metal-forming dies and press-tool parts) are Section 232 fixed-industrial-equipment derivatives at a 15% total rate; the other 45 are not on the lists and pay the 2026 Section 301 duty. The largest import group of the chapter.

productGroups.label: Knives and cutting blades for machines (metalworking, woodworking, food-industry and agricultural machines, lawnmower blades)
productGroups.blurb: All Free and not on the Section 232 lists, so only the 2026 Section 301 duties and China's List 3 apply.

productGroups.label: Unmounted plates, sticks, tips and inserts of cemented carbide or cermets
productGroups.blurb: 4.6% (Free for most FTA partners and Japan). Not on the Section 232 lists. Canadian carbide inserts pay 50% under Section 338 even with a USMCA claim.

productGroups.label: Hand-operated food and drink appliances of 10 kg or less (grinders, mills, slicers, can openers)
productGroups.blurb: 3.7%, not on the Section 232 lists; China adds 25% + 12.5%.

productGroups.label: Knives (table, kitchen, butcher, hunting, pocket and folding knives, multi-tools), knife sets, blades and handles
productGroups.blurb: Mostly a few cents each plus 2.2% to 10.6%. Every line is a Section 232 derivative steel article at 25% on the full value (9903.82.09), from every country and on top of any FTA rate. Knife sets (8211.10) pay the rate of the highest-rated knife in the set. Switchblade, gravity and ballistic knives may not be imported.

productGroups.label: Razors and razor blades, including blanks in strips
productGroups.blurb: All Free and not on the Section 232 lists. Chinese razors pay 7.5% List 4A + 12.5%; Canadian razors (8212.10) pay 50% under Section 338.

productGroups.label: Scissors, tailors' shears and similar shears, and their blades
productGroups.blurb: 1.7¢ to 8¢ each plus 3% to 8%. Not on the Section 232 lists and on no China list, so even Chinese scissors pay only the base rate + 12.5%.

productGroups.label: Other cutlery: letter openers, pencil sharpeners, nail clippers and files, manicure sets, cleavers, hair clippers
productGroups.blurb: 0.2¢ to 1.4¢ each plus 3.1% to 4.9%, or 4% to 4.1% (manicure sets in leather cases Free). Not on the Section 232 lists; most lines are on no China list.

productGroups.label: Spoons, forks, ladles, cake servers, butter knives, sugar tongs and similar flatware, and flatware sets
productGroups.blurb: From Free to 0.9¢ each + 15.8% (stainless spoons under 25¢: 14%). Every line is on the Section 232 list at 25% of the full value. Flatware sets (8215.10, 8215.20) pay the rate of the highest-rated piece in the set.

workedExamples.title: $50,000 of kitchen knives from China or Japan
workedExamples.body: Kitchen knives with plastic handles carry **0.8¢ each + 4.6%**. They are Section 232 derivative steel articles, so they pay **+25% of the full value** (9903.82.09) from any country. From Japan that is 0.8¢ each + 29.6%: about $14,800 on $50,000 plus 0.8¢ a knife; the 2026 Section 301 duty on Japan does not apply to Section 232 goods (note 52(f)(1)). From China, List 4A adds 7.5% (9903.88.15): **0.8¢ each + 37.1%**.

workedExamples.title: Socket wrenches from Taiwan, China or Canada
workedExamples.body: Base rate **9%**; wrenches are not on the Section 232 lists. From Taiwan the 2026 Section 301 rate is **10% in place of** the base rate (9903.05.76): **10%**. From China: 9% + 25% List 3 + 12.5% (9903.05.31) = **46.5%**. From Canada: **50%** under Section 338 (9903.03.14) even with a USMCA certificate, or 69% without one (9% + 10% + 50%).

workedExamples.title: A Chinese knife set, priced by its highest-rated knife
workedExamples.body: Sets of 8211.10 have no rate of their own: they pay **the rate of the knife in the set with the highest rate**, converted to an ad valorem equivalent where it is per-unit (Chapter 82 additional U.S. note 3), on the value of the whole set, plus **25%** Section 232 (8211.10 is on the list). In the tariff calculator you enter the 10-digit line of that knife, e.g. 8211.92.20.00 (0.8¢ each + 4.6%); the calculator applies its rate to the set's value and quantity and adds the set line's own Chapter 99 duties. 8211.10 is on no China Section 301 list, so a Chinese set pays the knife's rate + 25%.

workedExamples.title: Diamond saw blades from China
workedExamples.body: Free at base and not on the Section 232 list (only the blade cores, 8202.39.00.40, are). China pays 25% List 3 + 12.5% 2026 Section 301: **37.5%**. On top comes the **antidumping duty** of the diamond sawblades order (A-570-900), at the producer's cash-deposit rate; Commerce found in July 2026 that dumping margins up to 164.09% would likely recur without the order.

workedExamples.title: Carbide inserts from Canada, with or without USMCA
workedExamples.body: Base rate **4.6%**, Free under USMCA. Carbide inserts are on the Section 338 list (note 51(b)(3)), which applies even to USMCA goods: **50%** with a USMCA claim, **64.6%** without (4.6% + 10% Section 301 + 50%).

workedExamples.title: Press-tool parts from Germany
workedExamples.body: Base rate 2.9%, but this line is a Section 232 fixed-industrial-equipment derivative: the duty is topped up to **15% in total** (9903.82.10), from every country. With at least 85% U.S.-melted steel the total is 10% (9903.82.07). From January 1, 2028 the line moves to the 25% Section 232 rate (Proclamation 11021).

workedExamples.title: Stainless steel spoons from Vietnam
workedExamples.body: Stainless spoons valued under 25¢ each pay **14%**, plus **25%** Section 232: **39%**. The 12.5% Section 301 duty on Vietnam does not stack on Section 232 goods.

notes.chapterNotes:
**Note 1.** Apart from blow torches and similar self-contained torches, portable forges, grinding wheels with frameworks, manicure or pedicure sets, and goods of heading 8209, this chapter covers only articles with a blade, working edge, working surface or other working part of: (a) base metal; (b) metal carbides or cermets; (c) precious or semiprecious stones (natural, synthetic or reconstructed) on a support of base metal, metal carbide or cermet; or (d) abrasive materials on a support of base metal, provided that the articles have cutting teeth, flutes, grooves or the like, of base metal, which retain their identity and function after the application of the abrasive.

**Note 2.** Parts of base metal of the articles of this chapter are classified with the articles of which they are parts, except parts separately specified as such and toolholders for handtools (heading 8466). Parts of general use as defined in note 2 to section XV are always excluded. Heads, blades and cutting plates for electric shavers and electric hair clippers are classified in heading 8510.

**Note 3.** Sets consisting of one or more knives of heading 8211 and at least an equal number of articles of heading 8215 are classified in heading 8215.
notes.additionalUsNotes:
**1.** Provisions that refer to kitchen or tableware include articles of types used outdoors as well as indoors.

**2.** The length of files and rasps (heading 8203) does not include the tang.

**Statistical notes.** For sets of 8205, 8206, 8211 or 8215, report the total number of separate pieces. "Sheath-type knives" (8211.92) are fixed-blade knives in a substantial holster (sheath) of a kind used in hunting and fishing.

tariffUpdates.h1: HTS Chapter 82: Tools, Cutlery, Spoons and Forks of Base Metal — Tariff Updates

seo.title: Hand Tool, Knife & Cutlery Tariff Updates 2025–2026: Section 232 Derivatives, Section 301, Canada 338 (HTS Ch. 82) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: Every U.S. tariff change on HTS Chapter 82 tools and cutlery since 2025, with Federal Register citations: knives and flatware added to Section 232 in August 2025 and charged 25% on full value since April 6, 2026, the 2026 Section 301 duties on other tools, Section 338 on Canada, the end of IEEPA, and the diamond sawblades AD order.

tariffUpdates.intro:
This page compares the **2025 Basic Edition** (in force January 1, 2025) with the current **2026 Revision 21** (in force October 9, 2026) and lists every extra duty that reaches Chapter 82 today. No base rate changed and no line was added or renumbered: all 189 lines carry the same rates.

The extra duties changed completely. In January 2025 Chinese tools paid Section 301 (25% or 7.5%), Russian goods column 2 rates, and everyone else only the base rate. In 2025 the IEEPA duties (reciprocal, Canada, Mexico, China) reached the whole chapter, and on **August 18, 2025** Commerce added knives, flatware, vises and clamps, pipe and bolt cutters, certain edged tools, diamond sawblade cores and three die lines to Section 232 as derivative steel articles (50% on the steel content). The IEEPA duties ended on **February 24, 2026**; Proclamation 11021 moved Section 232 to the **full customs value** on **April 6, 2026** (25% for the 52 knife, flatware and tool lines, 15% total for the 3 die lines). Since July 2026 the 134 lines outside Section 232 pay the 2026 Section 301 duties on 60 economies and Brazil, and since August 22, 2026 Canada's wrenches, pliers, saw blades, carbide inserts and razors pay 50% under Section 338.

Two antidumping orders cover Chapter 82 goods from China, on **diamond sawblades** (continued after a 2026 sunset review) and **heavy forged hand tools**. They are company-specific, summarized below, and **not included in the tariff calculator**.
tariffUpdates.scope: Chapter 99 measures that reach Chapter 82 from any country: Section 232 derivative steel articles (note 16), China Section 301 (note 20), the 2026 Section 301 actions on 60 economies and Brazil (notes 50, 52), Canada Section 338 (note 51), Russia's rates in lieu of column 2 (note 30), the scheduled Nicaragua Section 301 duty (note 29), and the ended IEEPA and Section 122 duties. The Section 232 vehicle-part elections (certified auto and truck parts) are opt-in and left out. The antidumping orders on diamond sawblades and heavy forged hand tools from China are summarized for reference; the calculator does not model them. For the rate each supplier pays, see Rates by country.

inEffect.measure: Section 232 derivative steel articles, on the full customs value
inEffect.before: None until August 18, 2025; then +50% on the value of the steel content (inclusions list)
inEffect.exemption: Covers 52 lines on note 16(c)(vii): every knife line of 8211 (including knife sets, blades and handles), every flatware line of 8215 (including sets), vises and clamps (8205.70), other iron or steel hand tools of 8205.59.55, pipe cutters, bolt cutters and punches of 8203.40.60, and diamond sawblade cores (8202.39.00.40). No country exemptions; note 16(b) collects it on top of any FTA or USMCA rate. Because Chapter 82 is not chapter 72, 73, 74 or 76, the duty applies only when steel is at least 15% of the article's weight (9903.82.03), and articles with no steel at all are outside it (9903.82.01). Lower rates: UK goods with ≥95% UK-melted steel 15% (9903.82.05); ≥85% U.S.-melted steel 10% (9903.82.06). Goods under 9903.82.09 do not pay the 2026 Section 301 or Brazil duties (notes 52(f)(1), 50(a)(vi)(1)); China's 2018–2019 Section 301 lists still apply.

changes.title: No Chapter 82 base-rate changes
changes.detail: All 189 Chapter 82 lines carry the same general, special and column 2 rates in 2026 Revision 21 as in the 2025 Basic Edition; no line was added, split or renumbered.

changes.title: USTR keeps the China Section 301 tariffs
changes.detail: After the IEEPA ruling, USTR confirmed that the 2018–2019 Section 301 actions on China continue, so List 3 (25%) and List 4A (7.5%) still apply to Chapter 82 tools, knives and flatware.

changes.title: Section 338 list for Canada revised; Chapter 82 lines unchanged
changes.detail: Proclamation 11065 added and removed products on the note 51(b)(3) list and made the duty apply on top of Section 232. The 13 Chapter 82 subheadings stayed on the list and none of them is a Section 232 article, so their 50% did not change.

changes.title: Section 338: 50% on Canadian wrenches, pliers, saw blades, carbide inserts and razors
changes.detail: Proclamation 11048 imposed a 50% duty (9903.03.14) on products of Canada in the note 51(b)(3) list from August 22, 2026, after Proclamation 11056's three-day suspension. In Chapter 82 it reaches 18 lines: picks, hoes and rakes, steel circular and chain saw blades, pliers, metal-cutting shears, wrenches and sockets, light hammers, other hand tools of 8205.59.80, tool sets, carbide inserts and razors. They do not apply to Section 232 goods (note 52(f)(1)), so in Chapter 82 they reach the 134 lines outside Section 232: wrenches, pliers, hammers, screwdrivers, saw blades, drill bits, carbide inserts, scissors and razors. USMCA goods are exempt.

changes.title: Section 122 surcharge expired
changes.detail: The 10% surcharge on products of all countries (9903.03.01) expired at the close of July 23, 2026. It did not apply to Section 232 goods (Proclamation 11012), so in Chapter 82 it had charged the tools outside Section 232.

changes.title: Section 301 tariff on Brazil: knives and flatware exempt, other tools not
changes.detail: The 25% duty on goods of Brazil (9903.05.01) took effect. Section 232 goods are excluded (note 50(a)(vi)(1)), so it reaches the 134 Chapter 82 lines outside Section 232.

changes.title: Diamond sawblades order: Commerce finds dumping would recur
changes.detail: In its expedited third sunset review of the antidumping order on diamond sawblades and parts from China (A-570-900), Commerce found that revocation would likely lead to dumping margins of up to 164.09%. The ITC scheduled its expedited review the same day. The order stays in force; no revocation has been published.

changes.title: Proclamation 11032: 85% U.S.-melted test
changes.detail: From June 8, 2026, a derivative article qualifies for the 10% rate (9903.82.06, or 10% in total for the die lines under 9903.82.07) when at least 85% of its steel content by weight was melted and poured in the United States; it had to be all of it. Chapter 82's 25% and 15% rates did not change.

changes.title: Commerce corrects the Section 232 annex
changes.detail: Commerce added heading 9903.82.01, so articles on the lists that contain no steel, aluminum or copper pay no Section 232 duty, effective April 6, 2026.

changes.title: Die and press-tool lines move to the 25% Section 232 rate on January 1, 2028
changes.detail: Proclamation 11021 set a temporary 15% total rate for fixed industrial equipment derivatives (Annex III) until December 31, 2027; from January 1, 2028 they take the standard rates: 25% (9903.82.09), 15% for UK goods with UK-melted steel, 10% with U.S.-melted steel. In Chapter 82 that is 8207.20.00.70, 8207.30.60.62 and 8207.30.60.95.

changes.title: Section 232 on full value: knives and flatware 25%, die lines 15% (Proclamation 11021)
changes.detail: Proclamation 11021 replaced the earlier headings with 9903.82.02–9903.82.26, charged on the full customs value. In Chapter 82 the 52 knife, flatware, vise and clamp, cutter, edged-tool and sawblade-core lines move to the 25% list (Annex I-B, 9903.82.09) and the 3 die and press-tool lines to the 15% total rate for industrial equipment (Annex III). For goods other than chapters 72, 73, 74 and 76 the duty applies only when the metal is at least 15% of the weight. Manufacturing drawback is allowed for these goods from trade-agreement partners when they are not AD/CVD merchandise; goods admitted to a foreign-trade zone must take privileged foreign status.

changes.title: Third sunset review of the diamond sawblades order begins
changes.detail: Commerce initiated, and the ITC instituted, the five-year review of the antidumping order on diamond sawblades and parts from China.

changes.title: Section 122 surcharge replaces the IEEPA tariffs; Section 232 goods outside it
changes.detail: A 10% surcharge on products of all countries (9903.03.01) applied until July 23, 2026. It did not apply in addition to Section 232 duties, so in Chapter 82 only the lines outside Section 232 paid it; USMCA goods were exempt.

changes.title: All IEEPA tariffs end
changes.detail: After the Supreme Court held on February 20, 2026 (Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump) that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs, Executive Order 14389 ended the Canada, Mexico, China and reciprocal duties, and CBP stopped collecting them from 12:00 a.m. ET on February 24, 2026. Section 232 and Section 301 duties are not IEEPA duties and continued.

changes.title: Section 301 tariff on Nicaragua phases in from 2027
changes.detail: Products of Nicaragua that are not CAFTA-DR originating goods will pay +10% from January 1, 2027 and +15% from January 1, 2028 (9903.89.01, U.S. note 29). The rate is 0% in 2026.

changes.title: Knives, flatware, vises and other tools become Section 232 steel derivatives
changes.detail: Commerce's first inclusions round added to the derivative steel list the Chapter 82 provisions for knives and knife sets (8211), flatware and flatware sets (8215), vises and clamps (8205.70), other iron or steel hand tools (8205.59.55), pipe and bolt cutters (8203.40.60), diamond sawblade cores (8202.39.00.40) and three die lines of 8207.20 and 8207.30. They paid 50% (Proclamation 10947) on the value of their steel content; the non-steel content paid the IEEPA duties.

changes.title: Reciprocal tariff reaches Chapter 82
changes.detail: Executive Order 14257 set the reciprocal tariffs from April 5, 2025. No Chapter 82 line was on its Annex II exemption list, so all Chapter 82 goods paid it (Canada and Mexico aside). Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: IEEPA duties on Canada and Mexico
changes.detail: +25% on goods of Canada (9903.01.10) and Mexico (9903.01.01) from March 4, 2025; USMCA goods exempt from March 7, 2025. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: IEEPA duties on China
changes.detail: An additional 10% on all products of China from February 4, 2025, raised to 20% on March 4, 2025, on top of Section 301. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Heavy forged hand tools orders continued
changes.detail: Commerce continued the four antidumping orders on heavy forged hand tools from China (hammers and sledges over 1.5 kg, bars over 18 inches and wedges, picks and mattocks, axes and adzes) after its fifth sunset review, which found margins likely to prevail of 15.02% to 50.81%.

changes.title: Diamond sawblades order continued after the second sunset review
changes.detail: The antidumping order on diamond sawblades and parts from China was continued for another five years.

changes.title: China Section 301 List 4A cut to 7.5%
changes.detail: List 4A (9903.88.15), which took effect September 1, 2019 at 15% and covers Chinese table and kitchen knives, razors, some manicure items and flatware, was cut to 7.5% from February 14, 2020.

changes.title: China Section 301 List 3 raised to 25%
changes.detail: Chinese hand tools, saw blades, wrenches, drill bits, machine knives, carbide inserts and some knife and flatware lines (List 3, 9903.88.03) have paid Section 301 since September 24, 2018 at 10%, raised to 25% from May 10, 2019.

understandIndustry.why:
U.S. imports of Chapter 82 tools and cutlery were **$11.24B in 2025**, -1.7% from $11.43B in 2024 (peak: $12.67B in 2022). The five largest suppliers were China ($2.91B), Taiwan ($1.21B), Germany ($1.15B), Vietnam ($782M), Japan ($770M); Taiwan is reported to UN Comtrade as "Other Asia, nes". By product group the largest were drill bits & interchangeable tools (8207, $3.03B), hammers, screwdrivers & other hand tools (8205, $1.42B), carbide inserts & tips (8209, $1.07B). Knives and flatware (8211, 8215), which make up most of the Section 232 lines, were $1.40B.

China's shipments fell from $3.29B in 2024 to $2.91B in 2025, while Vietnam, Japan and Germany grew. In 2025 Chinese tools paid Section 301 plus the IEEPA duties; from August 18 knives and flatware from every country also paid the Section 232 steel duty. Since 2026 the IEEPA duties are gone, knives and flatware pay 25% of their full value, and the other tools pay the 2026 Section 301 duty of their country. The largest single six-digit line was 8209.00 ($1.07B).

2025 is the latest full year of U.S. trade data. Duty-collected figures aren't available from an official source yet.

seo.shortDescription: The total U.S. tariff on Chapter 82 tools and cutlery by country and product: 25% Section 232 on knives and flatware from everywhere, the 2026 Section 301 rates on other tools, China up to 37.5% extra, Canadian wrenches and carbide inserts 50%, USMCA and FTA effects.

industryAreas.intro:
Each cell is the base rate for that product group plus the extra duties for that country, minus any preference, from the current tariff schedule. Chapter 82 splits in two. **Knives and flatware** (and vises, clamps, some cutters and edged tools) are Section 232 derivative steel articles: **25%** on top of the base rate from every country, with or without an FTA claim, and no 2026 Section 301 duty. **All other tools** pay the 2026 Section 301 duty of their country: 10% or 12.5% added for most, 10% (EU, Taiwan) or 12.5% (Japan, Korea, Switzerland) *in place of* a lower base rate, nothing for USMCA goods.

China pays **25% (List 3) or 7.5% (List 4A)** more on most lines, plus 12.5% on the tools outside Section 232. Canada's wrenches, pliers, saw blades, carbide inserts, tool sets and razors pay **50%** under Section 338, even with USMCA. Brazil pays 37.5% extra on tools outside Section 232. Sets show the set rate as written (the rate of the highest-rated article). The table does **not** include antidumping duties on Chinese diamond sawblades and heavy forged hand tools (see Tariff updates).

tariffEngineering.h1: HTS Chapter 82: Tools, Cutlery, Spoons and Forks of Base Metal — Import Documents & Ways to Lower Duty

seo.title: Importing Hand Tools & Knives: Marking Rules, Switchblade Ban, Section 232 Entry, Sets & Ways to Lower Duty (HTS Ch. 82) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: The rules for each HTS Chapter 82 line: permanent origin marking on knives, scissors, pliers and razors, the switchblade import ban, Section 232 headings and the 15% metal-weight test, how sets are rated, AD scope, plus the legal ways to pay less: U.S.- or UK-melted steel, USMCA and FTA claims, origin, drawback.

tariffEngineering.intro:
Most Chapter 82 paperwork is about **marking** and **classification**. Knives, forks, scissors, shears, clippers, razors and blades, pliers and pincers must carry their country of origin **permanently** (die stamping, cast-in-mold lettering, etching, engraving or an attached metal plate; 19 CFR 134.43), or pay a 10% marking duty. Switchblade, gravity and ballistic knives may not be imported. Section 232 lines report 9903.82.09 (or a lower-rate heading) next to the Chapter 82 line and the country where the steel was melted and poured. Sets pay the rate of their highest-rated article (additional U.S. note 3).

The legal ways to pay less: **U.S.-melted** steel (10%), **UK-melted** steel (15%), the **15% metal-weight** test for articles that are mostly not steel, **USMCA** and FTA claims on the tools outside Section 232, avoiding **Chinese origin**, **drawback** on Section 232 duty from trade-agreement partners, and checking **antidumping scope** for diamond sawblades and heavy forged tools. Each rule and lever links to its regulation or proclamation.

levers.title: Use U.S.-melted steel in knives, flatware and other listed tools
levers.saves: 15 points on the 25% list (10% instead of 25%, 9903.82.06); 5 points on the die lines (10% instead of 15% in total, 9903.82.07)
levers.appliesTo: The 55 Section 232 lines: knives (8211), flatware (8215), vises and clamps, 8205.59.55 tools, 8203.40.60 cutters, diamond sawblade cores and the three die lines
levers.document: Mill certificates and supplier declarations showing that at least 85% (by weight) of the steel was melted and poured in the United States; reported in ACE.
levers.caveat: The 85% test applies from June 8, 2026 (before that, all of it). Origin and the base rate do not change; China's Section 301 duty still applies to Chinese-made goods.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 16(e), headings 9903.82.06 and 9903.82.07

levers.title: Buy UK knives and flatware made of UK-melted steel
levers.appliesTo: The 52 Section 232 lines on the 25% list, for products of the United Kingdom
levers.document: Mill test certificates and melt-and-pour reporting showing that at least 95% of the steel was melted and poured in the UK.
levers.caveat: The die lines have no UK rate (15% in total). Without the 95% proof UK goods pay 25%.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 16(d)

levers.title: Check the 15% metal-weight test
levers.saves: The whole Section 232 duty when steel is under 15% of the article's weight (9903.82.03) or absent (9903.82.01)
levers.appliesTo: The 55 Section 232 lines of Chapter 82 (the test does not exist for chapters 72, 73, 74 and 76, but does for Chapter 82)
levers.document: Bill of materials and weights showing the steel (plus any aluminum or copper on the lists) is less than 15% of the article's total weight; report 9903.82.03.
levers.caveat: Rare for knives and flatware, whose blade or body is the heaviest part; heavy wooden, plastic or ceramic handles or presentation boxes can matter for sets. When the duty does not apply, the 2026 Section 301 duty of the country applies instead.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 16(c), headings 9903.82.01 and 9903.82.03

levers.title: Know how sets are rated
levers.saves: The gap between the highest rate in a set and the rates of its other articles
levers.document: A list of every article in the set with its 10-digit line, rate and value. A set pays the highest rate (per-unit rates converted to ad valorem equivalents, additional U.S. note 3) on its whole value; articles imported loose are classified one by one. A CBP binding ruling settles whether goods are a set put up for retail sale.
levers.caveat: Classification follows how the goods are presented at import, not the importer's choice. Knife sets with at least as many 8215 pieces go to 8215 (Chapter 82 note 3). Section 232 and Section 301 duties follow the set's own line.

citations.label: HTSUS Chapter 82, note 3 and additional U.S. note 3

levers.title: Avoid Chinese origin
levers.saves: 25% (List 3) or 7.5% (List 4A), plus 12.5% on tools outside Section 232, and any antidumping duty on diamond sawblades or heavy forged tools
levers.appliesTo: Almost every Chapter 82 line, for goods of China
levers.document: Production records showing where the article was made; origin follows the last substantial transformation (for goods processed in Canada or Mexico, the tariff-shift rules of 19 CFR 102.20). Ask CBP for a binding ruling.
levers.caveat: Assembling Chinese diamond sawblade cores and segments in a third country has been found to circumvent the AD order (Thailand, Canada). Other countries pay the 2026 Section 301 duty or Section 232 instead.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 20

levers.title: Claim USMCA on Canadian and Mexican tools
levers.saves: The base rate and the 10% Section 301 duty (9903.05.93, 9903.05.94) on tools outside Section 232; the base rate on knives and flatware
levers.appliesTo: Originating goods of Canada or Mexico
levers.document: A USMCA certification of origin from the importer, exporter or producer, available to CBP on request.
levers.caveat: A USMCA claim does not reduce Section 232 (note 16(b)) or the 50% Section 338 duty on the 13 Canadian subheadings (note 51(a)).

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. notes 51 and 52

levers.title: Claim the FTA rate (Korea, Israel, Australia, Chile, Colombia and others)
levers.saves: The base rate (up to 12% or a few cents each plus a percentage)
levers.appliesTo: Lines whose special column lists the partner's code (AU, BH, CL, CO, IL, JO, KR, MA, OM, P, PA, PE, SG; JP on some 8207 and 8209 lines)
levers.document: The FTA's origin documentation (certification or knowledge of origin) under the agreement's CBP regulations.
levers.caveat: Section 232 still applies on top (note 16(b)), and the 2026 Section 301 duty is added for Israel and other partners, or replaces the base rate for Korea (12.5% in place). GSP has lapsed.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 16(b)

levers.title: Drawback of Section 232 duty from trade-agreement partners
levers.saves: Up to 99% of the Section 232 duty on goods used in exported products, plus ordinary duties on any line
levers.appliesTo: Section 232 lines (Annex I-B and Annex III) that are products of the UK, EU, Japan, Korea, Mexico or Canada, whose steel was melted in one of them, and that are not AD/CVD merchandise
levers.document: A drawback claim to CBP with import and export records (19 CFR part 191).
levers.caveat: Diamond sawblade cores (8202.39.00.40) are AD merchandise and cannot use it. AD/CVD are never refundable (19 CFR 191.3).

levers.title: Check antidumping scope before you buy
levers.saves: The whole antidumping duty, when the product or producer is outside the order

levers.document: The order's written scope (it, not the HTS number, decides; e.g. resin-bonded or electroplated blades without a diamond segment, and hammers with heads of 1.5 kg or less, are outside) and the producer's cash-deposit rate; when unsure, request a scope ruling from Commerce.
levers.caveat: A product in scope pays the cash deposit even if entered under another HTS line. Rates change with each administrative review.

finalConclusion.intro: Straight answers to the most-searched questions about U.S. tariffs on tools, knives and cutlery (HTS Chapter 82), by product, by country and by HS code. Each answer links to the page with the detail and the official sources.
keyTakeaways: Knives (8211) and spoons, forks and flatware (8215), plus vises, clamps, some cutters, edged tools and diamond sawblade cores, are Section 232 derivative steel articles: 25% of the full value from every country, on top of the base rate and any FTA or USMCA claim. The other 134 lines (wrenches, pliers, hammers, screwdrivers, saw blades, drill bits, carbide inserts, scissors, razors) pay the 2026 Section 301 duty: 10% or 12.5% for most countries, 10% or 12.5% in place of a lower base rate for the EU, Taiwan, Japan, Korea and Switzerland, nothing for USMCA goods.

China adds 25% (List 3) or 7.5% (List 4A) on most lines; Canadian wrenches, pliers, saw blades, carbide inserts, tool sets and razors pay 50% under Section 338 even with USMCA. Diamond sawblades and heavy forged hand tools from China also carry antidumping duties. The IEEPA tariffs ended February 24, 2026.
In 2025 the U.S. imported $11.24B of Chapter 82 goods; China ($2.91B) and Taiwan ($1.21B) were the largest suppliers.

faqs.question: What is HTS Chapter 82?
faqs.answer: Chapter 82 of the Harmonized Tariff Schedule covers tools, implements, cutlery, spoons and forks of base metal: garden and farm hand tools (8201), saws and blades (8202), files, pliers and cutters (8203), wrenches (8204), other hand tools and vises (8205), tool sets (8206), interchangeable tools such as drill bits and dies (8207), machine knives (8208), carbide inserts (8209), hand-operated kitchen appliances (8210), knives (8211), razors (8212), scissors (8213), other cutlery such as clippers (8214) and flatware (8215). It has 189 ten-digit lines; power tools are in Chapter 84 or 85.

faqs.question: What is the HTS code for knives?
faqs.answer: Knives are heading 8211: table knives with fixed blades 8211.91 (steak knives 8211.91.50.30 or .80.30), kitchen, chef and butcher knives 8211.92.20 (plastic or rubber handles) or 8211.92.90, hunting and sheath knives 8211.92.40 / .60 / .90.45, pocket, folding and multi-tool knives 8211.93, blades 8211.94, handles 8211.95 and knife sets 8211.10. Machine knives are 8208 and butter and fish knives 8215.

faqs.question: What is the tariff on knives from Japan, China or Germany?
faqs.answer: Every knife line is a Section 232 derivative steel article, so knives pay **25% of their value** on top of the base rate from any country, FTA or not. A kitchen knife of 8211.92.20 (0.8¢ each + 4.6%) pays 0.8¢ each + 29.6% from Japan or Germany (the 2026 Section 301 duty does not stack on Section 232 goods) and 0.8¢ each + 37.1% from China (List 4A adds 7.5%). Knives made from at least 85% U.S.-melted steel pay 10% instead of 25%; UK knives with UK-melted steel 15%.

faqs.question: What is the tariff on Swiss Army and other pocket knives?
faqs.answer: Pocket and folding knives, including multi-tool knives, are 8211.93 at 3¢ each + 5.4%, plus 25% Section 232: **3¢ each + 30.4%** from Switzerland or anywhere else. Switzerland's 12.5% Section 301 rate does not apply to Section 232 goods. Spring-opening (switchblade), gravity and ballistic knives cannot be imported at all.

faqs.question: What is the tariff code for cutlery and stainless steel flatware?
faqs.answer: Spoons, forks, ladles, cake servers, butter knives and similar flatware are 8215: stainless spoons 8215.99.30 (14% if under 25¢ each) or .35 (6.8%), stainless forks 8215.99.01–.15, plated pieces 8215.91, and sets 8215.10 (with a plated piece) or 8215.20. A set of table knives with at least as many forks or spoons is classified in 8215, not 8211 (Chapter 82 note 3). Every 8215 line pays 25% Section 232 on top of the base rate.

faqs.question: What is the tariff code for hand tools?
searchedAs: hs code for hand tools spanners
faqs.answer: Hand tools are spread over 8201–8205: garden tools 8201, saws 8202, files, pliers and cutters 8203, wrenches and sockets 8204 (9%), and hammers 8205.20, screwdrivers 8205.40, household tools 8205.51, vises and clamps 8205.70 and other hand tools 8205.59. Most are outside Section 232 and pay their base rate plus the 2026 Section 301 duty; vises, clamps and 8205.59.55 tools pay 25% Section 232. Power tools are not in Chapter 82 (8467).

faqs.question: What are the tariffs on hand tools from China?
searchedAs: what are the tariffs on china
faqs.answer: Most Chinese tools pay their base rate + 25% Section 301 List 3 + 12.5% under the 2026 Section 301 action: a socket wrench pays **46.5%**. Knives and flatware pay 25% Section 232 plus 7.5% (List 4A) or 25% (List 3) where listed. Scissors are on no China list and pay only the base rate + 12.5% (3¢ each + 15.5% for 8213.00.90). Chinese diamond sawblades and heavy forged hand tools also carry antidumping duties. China shipped $2.91B of Chapter 82 goods in 2025.

faqs.question: Where does the U.S. import hand tools and cutlery from?
faqs.answer: In 2025 the United States imported $11.24B of Chapter 82 tools and cutlery. The largest suppliers were China ($2.91B), Taiwan ($1.21B), Germany ($1.15B), Vietnam ($782M), Japan ($770M). The biggest product groups were drill bits & interchangeable tools (8207, $3.03B), hammers, screwdrivers & other hand tools (8205, $1.42B), carbide inserts & tips (8209, $1.07B).

faqs.question: Which Chapter 82 products are on the Section 232 steel derivatives list?
searchedAs: what items are affected by tariffs
what items are included in the tariffs
faqs.answer: Note 16(c) to Chapter 99 lists 55 Chapter 82 lines: all knives and knife sets, blades and handles (8211), all spoons, forks and flatware sets (8215), vises and clamps (8205.70), other iron or steel hand tools of 8205.59.55, pipe cutters, bolt cutters and punches of 8203.40.60 and diamond sawblade cores (8202.39.00.40), at 25%; and parts of drawing dies, metal-forming dies and press-tool parts of 8207.20 and 8207.30, at 15% in total. They were added on August 18, 2025. Wrenches, pliers, hammers, saw blades, drill bits, scissors and razors are not on the list.

faqs.question: What is the HS code and duty for a tool set or socket set?
searchedAs: hs code for socket wrench set
hts code for drill bit set
faqs.answer: Sets of tools from two or more of headings 8202–8205 put up for retail sale are 8206; sets of one kind of 8205 tool are 8205.90.60, and a socket set of only sockets and drives is 8204.20 (9%). Sets of 8206 and 8205.90.60 have no rate of their own: they pay the rate of the article in the set with the highest rate (per-unit rates converted to ad valorem equivalents) on the whole set. In the tariff calculator, enter the 10-digit line of that article. Canadian 8206 sets pay 50% Section 338.

faqs.question: What is the HS code and tariff for drill bits?
searchedAs: hs code for hss drill bits
faqs.answer: Drill bits are 8207.50 (masonry drills 8207.50.20.30, twist drills 8207.50.20.45/.55 or 8207.50.40.30), rock-drilling bits 8207.13 and 8207.19. Most pay 5% or 8.4% and are outside Section 232: a German twist drill pays **10%** (the EU rate of 10% in place of the base rate), a Chinese one **42.5%** (5% + 25% + 12.5%).

faqs.question: What is the HTS code for scissors?
faqs.answer: Scissors, tailors' shears and similar shears are 8213.00: 1.7¢ each + 4.3% if valued at $1.75 a dozen or less, 8¢ each + 8% for pinking shears over $30 a dozen, and 3¢ each + 3% for other scissors. They are outside Section 232 and on no China Section 301 list, so most countries add only the 2026 Section 301 duty. Scissors must be marked with their country of origin by stamping, etching or engraving.

faqs.question: What is the tariff code for carbide inserts?
faqs.answer: Unmounted plates, sticks, tips and inserts of sintered carbide are 8209.00.00.30 (other cermets .60), at 4.6% (Free for most FTA partners and Japan). They are outside Section 232. Canadian inserts pay 50% under Section 338 even with USMCA (50%); EU and Taiwanese inserts 10%, Japanese inserts Free base but 12.5% under the 2026 Section 301 action.

faqs.question: Which Chapter 82 products are on the Section 338 Canada list?
faqs.answer: Note 51(b)(3) lists 13 Chapter 82 subheadings at 50% (9903.03.14) since August 22, 2026: 8201.30, 8202.31, 8202.40.60, 8203.20.60, 8203.30, 8204.11, 8204.12, 8204.20, 8205.20.30, 8205.59.80, 8206, 8209 and 8212.10. The duty applies even to USMCA-qualifying goods; other Canadian tools are Free with USMCA, and Canadian knives and flatware pay 25% Section 232. Canada shipped $376M of Chapter 82 goods in 2025.

faqs.question: Are there antidumping duties on diamond saw blades?
faqs.answer: Yes, from China. The antidumping order on diamond sawblades and parts (cores and segments), A-570-900, has applied since November 2009; Commerce found in its July 2026 sunset review that margins up to 164.09% would likely recur, and the order stays in force. Blades assembled in Thailand and Canada by two firms were found to circumvent it. The blades are 8202.39.00.10 (Free + 37.5% from China), cores 8202.39.00.40 (also 25% Section 232), sets 8206.
